slides.text:
Rust has two float types for numbers with a fractional part: `f32` and `f64`. `f64` is the default and the one to use unless memory matters.

Floats are stored in binary, so many decimal values are close approximations, not exact.
A number is a float only when it is written like one: `2.0` is a float, `2` is an integer. Rust never converts between them on its own.
You will write float literals and arithmetic, print floats with a fixed number of decimals, meet the surprises of binary storage, and use the methods floats come with.

A literal with a decimal point is a float, and without a type it is an `f64`. Add a type to choose `f32`.

Unlike integers, dividing floats keeps the fraction.

exercises.title: Float variables
exercises.guide: Declare two floats, price three items and print.

chunks.guide: `price` is an `f64`, the default float type. `rate` asks for the smaller `f32`.
chunks.text:
let price: f64 = 20.5;
    let rate: f32 = 0.5;

chunks.guide: A float times a float literal stays a float: three items at that price.
Print the three values with `{}`.

exercises.title: Write the weight
exercises.guide: Write the weight so that `ratio` prints `0.0725`.

exercises.title: Dividing floats
exercises.guide: Divide two floats, then combine the result.

chunks.guide: A bill to split between two people.
Float division keeps the fraction, with no rounding down.
chunks.text:
let share = bill / people;
    println!("{}", share);

chunks.guide: `*` runs before `-`, with floats as with integers.
chunks.text:
let rest = bill - share * 1.5;
    println!("{}", rest);

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: Integer division drops the fraction, so `7 / 2` is `3`. With floats, `7.0 / 2.0` is `3.5`.

exercises.title: Ways to write a float
exercises.guide: Write floats with separators, exponents and a suffix.

chunks.guide: Underscores split long numbers and change nothing.

notes.text: Underscores are ignored, only for reading.

chunks.guide: `e` means times ten to a power. An exponent alone makes a float, even with no decimal point.

notes.text: 2.5 times ten to the power of minus 3.
3 times ten to the 8th, still a float.

chunks.guide: A suffix sets the type of a literal.

notes.text: Same as writing the type on the variable.

chunks.guide: Print the four values.

exercises.title: Which one compiles?
exercises.guide: Pick the expression that compiles in the blank.
exercises.explanation: Rust never converts between integers and floats by itself, so both sides must be floats: `3.0 * 1.5`.

slides.text:
A float prints with as many digits as it needs. `{:.2}` fixes the digits after the point, and rounds to fit.

Binary storage means some results carry a tiny error.

exercises.title: Fixed decimals
exercises.guide: Print a total with a set number of decimals.

chunks.guide: A price and a quantity.
`.2` after the colon asks for two digits after the point.
chunks.text:
let total = price * qty;
    println!("{:.2}", total);

chunks.guide: One decimal rounds the value further.

exercises.title: Print a receipt
exercises.guide: Print the total the way a receipt shows money, so `13.5` appears as `13.50`.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: The value is rounded, not cut: `2.72` for two decimals, and `3` when none are asked.

exercises.title: Adding 0.1 and 0.2
exercises.guide: Add two simple floats and look at what is stored.

chunks.guide: Two values that look exact. In binary, neither one is.
Without a precision, every stored digit shows.
Two decimals hide the tiny error.

exercises.title: Two sizes of float
exercises.guide: Store the same division in both float types.

chunks.guide: The same division, once per type.
chunks.text:
let wide: f64 = 1.0 / 3.0;
    let narrow: f32 = 1.0 / 3.0;

chunks.guide: The `f32` keeps fewer digits.

exercises.title: Dividing by zero
exercises.guide: Divide floats by zero and print what comes out.

chunks.guide: A float zero in a variable.
Float division by zero does not panic, unlike integer division. It gives a special value.
Print the three results.

slides.text:
A float has methods, called with a dot after the value. The value needs a known float type, so `2.0.cbrt()` does not compile: put it in a variable with a type first.

`cbrt` is the cube root.
slides.code:
let x: f64 = 8.0;
let y = x.cbrt();

slides.text: Several methods round a float, and each one treats the fractional part differently. Negative numbers show the difference best.

exercises.title: Roots and powers
exercises.guide: Use methods to take a root and raise to powers.

chunks.guide: The type is written so methods can be called on it.
`powi` takes a whole-number exponent, `powf` a float one. A power of 0.5 is a square root.
Print each one with one decimal.

exercises.title: Pick the methods
exercises.guide: Take the square root, then the whole-number power of 3, not the float one.

exercises.title: Four ways to round
exercises.guide: Round one negative number four different ways.

chunks.guide: A negative value with a half.
`floor` goes down, `ceil` goes up.
`round` goes to the nearest, halves away from zero. `trunc` cuts the fraction.

notes.text: A half goes away from zero.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `floor` gives 3 and `round` gives 4. With `{}`, a float with no fractional part prints without `.0`.

exercises.title: Absolute value, min and max
exercises.guide: Compare two floats with their own methods.

chunks.guide: A negative float and another one.
`abs` drops the sign.
`min` and `max` take the other float as an argument and give back the smaller or larger.

exercises.title: Circle measures
exercises.guide: Use the built-in value of pi to measure a circle.

chunks.guide: `::` reaches into a path: here std, then f64, then consts.

notes.text: A ready-made constant, no import needed.

chunks.text:
let radius: f64 = 3.0;
    let pi = std::f64::consts::PI;

chunks.guide: The area is pi times the radius squared.
chunks.text:
let area = pi * radius.powi(2);
    println!("{:.2}", area);

chunks.guide: The circumference is two times pi times the radius.
chunks.text:
let edge = 2.0 * pi * radius;
    println!("{:.2}", edge);
